A compiler translates a program through several representations before producing machine instructions. A tensor program describes mathematical operations and shapes, while a lower representation also describes memory, loops, and the order of execution. Engineers inspect these representations to understand which transformations preserve the computation and which transformations change floating point rounding. Matrix multiplication often accounts for much of the arithmetic in a transformer, but moving data between layouts can also consume substantial time. A useful experiment keeps model weights, input tokens, thread count, and output requirements fixed while changing one implementation choice. The resulting embeddings should be checked against an independent reference before interpreting a timing difference. Measurements should retain individual observations so that variations between runs remain visible. A performance report should explain its timing boundary, whether initialization is included, and how it counts tokens in padded input. Clear records make it possible for another engineer to repeat an experiment and distinguish a compiler improvement from a change in the workload.

An observatory on a mountain collects measurements throughout the year. Its instruments record temperature, humidity, wind, and the brightness of the night sky. Researchers first check the instruments against known references, then preserve the original observations alongside processed results. Clouds and seasonal changes affect which observations can be compared directly. The team therefore records conditions and repeats measurements rather than assuming that two visits provide identical circumstances. A student preparing a report separates the uncertainty of an instrument from changes in the environment. Missing observations are marked explicitly and are never replaced with invented measurements. When an instrument is repaired, the team checks whether its readings remain compatible with the earlier record. Different instruments may describe the same event with different units, so conversions and assumptions must be documented. The value of the archive comes from its combination of useful measurements, clear methods, and enough context to understand the limits of each conclusion.

A public library is organizing a collection of letters, maps, journals, and technical manuals. The catalog must help readers find related material even when authors use different words for the same subject. Librarians preserve the original descriptions and add carefully reviewed metadata about language, date, and topic. Search results are evaluated using examples from several parts of the collection. A system that works well on short titles may behave differently on a long document containing several subjects. The team tests both individual documents and groups of documents, checking that the order of returned results matches the order of submitted requests. Empty descriptions, unusual punctuation, and documents near the length limit require explicit handling. When a search index is rebuilt, the librarians compare results against a saved reference collection. They record which settings changed and keep examples of both successful and unsuccessful searches. This process supports improvements while maintaining readers' ability to understand and trust the catalog.

A transport planning group studies how people move between homes, workplaces, schools, and public services. Its reports combine short questions with longer descriptions of routes and travel constraints. The same destination may be described by a street name, a landmark, or a neighborhood, so text matching alone does not always retrieve the most useful information. Analysts compare several search methods using the same collection of requests and documents. They examine each result rather than relying only on an average score that could hide a failure for one group of users. Experiments include requests of different lengths and batches containing distinct questions. The preparation of the test collection is recorded separately from the time spent answering a request. When a method is changed, the group repeats correctness checks before publishing new performance numbers. Reproducible inputs and clearly stated assumptions allow later studies to build on the work without confusing a change in the service with a change in the evaluation procedure.
